title: Image to Base64 Online: Original Files, Resizing, and Data URLs
description: Convert a local image to Base64. Learn how to keep the original file, resize the image, and choose between a full Data URL and raw Base64.
content:
Open the Image to Base64 converter, select a local image, click “Convert to Base64,” and copy the result. Use the full Data URL on a web page. If an API accepts only a Base64 string, take everything after the first comma. Leave the maximum width at 0 to preserve the original file bytes.

Check the prefix after converting an image

Select a file in the “Select Image” panel, leave the maximum width at its default, and click “Convert to Base64.” When you see “Conversion complete.” look for text starting with data: in the “Base64 Result” panel. The image preview appears below the result box. If you see “Please select an image first.”, select a file and try again.

Read the media type at the start of the result before copying it. With a PNG file and the default width, the result starts with data:image/png;base64, even if the format menu shows JPEG. Use the prefix to verify the actual output format. The result box is read-only. To extract a portion, copy the result into a temporary text buffer first.

What a maximum width of 0 preserves

When the maximum width is 0, the page uses FileReader to read the file and generate a Data URL.[S3] This path wraps the original file bytes. Text in the image, transparent areas, and embedded metadata are all preserved. The file picker shows the filename. The Data URL prefix only needs the media type and encoding marker.

The same image can have different delivery requirements across projects. Use the original-file path if an archive workflow needs to read capture metadata. Generate and save a smaller image separately for display. Anyone working with the display version can then refer back to the source file.

To deliver text that can reconstruct the original file, decode the part after the comma into a file and compare its bytes with the original. Similar previews only tell you that the images look similar. Compare the decoded bytes for deduplication or verification. When preserving the original, record the width setting with the output so you can repeat the conversion later.

Set the width before choosing a format

Set a positive maximum width to use the canvas path. If the browser can decode the image, the page draws the bitmap to a canvas, preserves its aspect ratio, and exports it in the selected format. It scales the image down only when the maximum width is smaller than the original width. To change the format while keeping the pixel dimensions, enter the original width, convert again, and verify the output prefix.

The quality setting applies to JPEG and WebP and defaults to 0.85. For PNG, the page calls the canvas export method without a quality argument. When comparing settings, use the same source image and change one field at a time. To keep the smaller image legible, inspect the smallest text or thinnest lines before reducing the width further.

When to use the full Data URL or just the Base64

If you only have a screenshot of the string, return to the result box and copy it again. The visible area next to the preview is limited, and transcribing it line by line can leave gaps. Paste the copied result into an editor, inspect both sides of the comma, and select the part the destination expects.

A Data URL uses a comma to separate the prefix from the data. In data:image/png;base64,, image/png is the media type and ;base64 indicates that the following data is Base64-encoded.[S1] For raw Base64, remove everything up to and including the first comma. Preserve trailing equals signs as required by the destination.[S2]

When integrating with another system, look at a sample field value. If it starts with data:, send the full string. If it shows only encoded characters, start after the comma. Some APIs use a separate media type field. Copy that value from the actual prefix and put the part after the comma in the data field.

DestinationWhat to sendWhat to verify
HTML image URL or CSS background URLFull Data URLThe prefix contains the media type and data follows the comma
API field that explicitly requires raw Base64Encoded data after the commaThe field value has no data: prefix
Workflow that needs to reconstruct the fileDecoded image bytesThe saved file type matches the actual output

Verify the result in HTML, CSS, or JSON

In HTML, put the full result inside the quotes of the image element’s src attribute. In CSS, pass it as the background-image value using url(). Open the final page to verify that the image displays. The tool’s preview only shows that the tool page has attempted to load the data.

To debug the page, open the browser’s element inspector and look at the rendered image URL. If the template has a value but the rendered element does not, trace how the value passes from the template to the component. If the element contains the full URL, look for browser errors.

When writing the string to JSON, let the serializer handle the surrounding quotes. You can also verify the structure with the JSON formatter. Once the syntax is valid, verify which string format the destination expects. To troubleshoot, send a small image through the same field first, then try the intended image. This helps distinguish a field mapping problem from a length limit.

Compare the KB estimate with the string length

Standard Base64 uses 4 characters to represent a group of up to 3 bytes. For 1024 bytes, the padded result is 1368 characters before the Data URL prefix.[S2] If the destination enforces a character limit, count the characters in the full string you plan to send. The image file size measures something different.

Choose a size metric before comparing compressed and uncompressed output. If an API takes the complete URL, compare the URL character counts. If a file storage service takes decoded images, compare the image byte counts. Use the metric that matches the destination to see whether changing the width helps.

The tool’s “Approx.” value estimates the image byte count from the full Data URL length and displays it in KB. The estimate includes the prefix. Use it to compare conversions of the same image. Do not treat it as the size of a JSON request body. For an exact decoded image size, decode the part after the comma and count the resulting bytes.

What Copy and Download result give you

“Copy” copies the current value in the result box, including the Data URL prefix and comma. Before sending it to a colleague for web testing, you can paste it into a plain-text editor and verify the beginning and end. If the destination expects the entire value in one field, select and paste the full string, including any text outside the visible area.

“Download result” uses the Data URL as the download address. The browser downloads the image bytes represented by that URL. The suggested filename in the source code has a text extension, so verify the actual media type before handing off the file. To save the string itself, copy it from the result box and save it as a text file.

Troubleshoot a blank preview

First, look for a comma in the result box and verify that data follows it. If the result is only data:,, the canvas export may have produced no writable image. The specification lists cases such as a canvas with no pixels or a serialization failure.[S4] Verify the dimensions, then set the width back to 0 and see if the original-file path produces a result with an image media type.

If the tool displays the image but the target page does not, inspect the URL that the target page received. Open the console in the target page’s developer tools. If the log says the Content Security Policy blocked the image, verify that img-src allows the URL.[S5] If the prefix is missing, fix the step that produces the URL so individual components do not have to reconstruct it.

Limits and fallback behavior

If image decoding fails, the page still tries to read the source file. This fallback may produce a string or show “Conversion complete.” even if the preview cannot display the image. Try opening the source image in your system image viewer. If it opens, retry with an image the browser can decode and verify the output before sending it.

A Data URL puts the entire image in a field, which may have a length limit.[S1] For large images, find out whether the destination accepts files or only strings. Base64 is reversible, so sharing the encoded string also shares its image bytes.[S2] If you intend to share only the processed image, verify that you copied the current result and remove the old result from what you plan to send.

Verify the output before sending it

You may need the same image for a web page and an API. Save the full result first, then extract the encoded data if the API requires it. To distinguish plain encoded text from an image URL with a prefix, compare the text examples in the Base64 encoder and decoder. To verify image bytes, decode them back into a file.

After a successful test, record whether you used the original-file path or the canvas path. Reuse the same settings when switching images. Verify the prefix for each image, especially if the source formats vary. Always copy from the result box after conversion.

  • If a web page needs the URL, verify that you pasted everything from data: through the end of the payload, then open the page to see if the image displays.
  • If an API needs raw Base64, verify that the field starts with the data after the comma and that any separate media type matches the original prefix.
  • If the destination has a size limit, measure the output the same way the destination does. Keep other settings fixed, change only the width or quality, and compare the results.

faqs.q: Why is the result still PNG when I select JPEG?
faqs.a: When the maximum width is 0, the tool reads the original file. Set a positive maximum width, verify that the browser can decode the source image, convert it again, and check the new output prefix.

faqs.q: Should I remove the data: prefix before sending the result to an API?
faqs.a: Follow the field requirements. For a full Data URL, keep the prefix and comma. For raw Base64, take only the encoded data after the first comma.
